source.text: וַ/יְכַ֤ל אֱלֹהִים֙ בַּ/יּ֣וֹם הַ/שְּׁבִיעִ֔י מְלַאכְתּ֖/וֹ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֑ה וַ/יִּשְׁבֹּת֙ בַּ/יּ֣וֹם הַ/שְּׁבִיעִ֔י מִ/כָּל מְלַאכְתּ֖/וֹ אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָֽׂה־׃

translation.text: On the seventh day[a] God finished his work that he had done[b], and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.

footnotes.text: The edited Samaritan Hebrew digital text and Rahlfs–Hanhart’s selected Greek text read ‘sixth’ for completion; both retain ‘seventh’ for cessation. The Masoretic base used here has ‘seventh’ in both clauses. In the published 4Q10 transcription, both day numerals are supplied, not surviving ink. Historical priority remains unresolved.

Alternatively, ‘By the seventh day God had finished his work.’ This understands completion retrospectively in light of 2:1. The main wording retains the repeated day phrase and does not itself imply additional creative work or work throughout the seventh day.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Finished preserves the active completion statement without choosing a retrospective English pluperfect in the main text. The connected narrative can summarize or specify completion; the alternative had finished remains plausible and is disclosed in note[b]. This is a local working preference, not a rule that wayyiqtol always maps to English simple past or proof of additional seventh-day creation. No fresh HALOT consultation is claimed.
In Genesis 1–2 this plural form regularly takes singular verbal agreement and refers to the one true God; standard English singular 'God' is required by the syntax and context.

On the seventh day preserves the same temporal phrase used with completion and cessation. By the seventh day is a plausible contextual interpretation, not an exclusive gloss dictated by ב; it is disclosed in note[b]. Note[a] distinguishes the sixth source alternative from this same-source English choice. Seventh is retained provisionally, not historically established as earliest. No fresh HALOT consultation is claimed.
מְלָאכָה denotes work, occupation, or labor. 'Work' is the most natural and contextually fitting English equivalent in the creation account.
עשה is a broad verb meaning do/make. 'That he had done' preserves the Hebrew wording closely and reads naturally in English, while avoiding unnecessary narrowing to material manufacture alone.

The verb שבת fundamentally means to cease. In this context, where cessation from creative work marks the sanctity of the seventh day, 'rested' is the established and contextually appropriate English rendering, while still implying cessation from labor rather than recovery from fatigue.
The preposition מן with כָּל is straightforwardly rendered 'from all,' indicating cessation with respect to the entirety of God's work.

theological_decisions.issue: Completion and cessation on the seventh day
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: The main English retains seventh-day completion and cessation; their temporal relationship is not resolved by a theological contradiction veto.
alternative_readings: By the seventh day God had finished his work as a retrospective interpretation
theological_decisions.rationale: Genesis2:1 gives a completed-state summary;2:2 may specify or explain completion together with cessation. The main preserves the repeated day phrase, with a plausible retrospective interpretation noted. Neither wording itself establishes a separate creative act throughout the seventh day. The sixth-day source alternative is disclosed separately and historical priority remains unresolved.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1 and 3; original-language primacy and preservation of theological tension

value.text: By the seventh day God had finished his work that he had done[a], and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.

footnotes.text: Literally, 'On the seventh day God finished his work.' The Hebrew wording is often rendered this way; 'By the seventh day' in the main text expresses the likely sense in context.

value.rationale: The verb כלה means to complete or finish. Because the clause is followed by 'on the seventh day' and then 'he rested on the seventh day,' English pluperfect ('had finished') best conveys the sense that the work was complete by the time the seventh day arrived, avoiding the misleading implication that God was still working during the seventh day.
In Genesis 1–2 this plural form regularly takes singular verbal agreement and refers to the one true God; standard English singular 'God' is required by the syntax and context.

Literally 'on the seventh day.' Here 'by the seventh day' is an optimal-equivalence rendering that reflects the temporal sense in context and harmonizes with the following statement that God rested on the seventh day. The literal alternative is preserved in a footnote because it is a notable translational option.
מְלָאכָה denotes work, occupation, or labor. 'Work' is the most natural and contextually fitting English equivalent in the creation account.
עשה is a broad verb meaning do/make. 'That he had done' preserves the Hebrew wording closely and reads naturally in English, while avoiding unnecessary narrowing to material manufacture alone.

The verb שבת fundamentally means to cease. In this context, where cessation from creative work marks the sanctity of the seventh day, 'rested' is the established and contextually appropriate English rendering, while still implying cessation from labor rather than recovery from fatigue.
The preposition מן with כָּל is straightforwardly rendered 'from all,' indicating cessation with respect to the entirety of God's work.

value.issue: Whether the text implies God worked during the seventh day
value.chosen_reading: The English main text renders the first clause as 'By the seventh day God had finished his work,' indicating completion by that day rather than activity continuing into it.
alternative_readings: 'On the seventh day God finished his work' as a more formally literal rendering of the Hebrew wording
value.rationale: The Hebrew phrase can be rendered literally as 'on the seventh day,' but in context this can sound contradictory with the next clause stating that God rested on the seventh day. Rendering the verb in English pluperfect and the phrase as 'by the seventh day' preserves the sense without importing a doctrinal claim beyond the text. The more literal wording is preserved in a footnote for auditability.
